title: Levy calculation process unclear
full_text:
The SMSF Association has welcomed the limited amount advisers will be required to pay as a special levy to fund the operation of the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR), but has criticised the lack of transparency in how that cost was allocated to the advice sector.
The professional body raised its concerns in a submission to Treasury on the CSLR 2026/27 special levy in which it reiterated a waterfall model based on the concept of a connected sub-sector was not a long-term solution to funding the scheme.
“We welcome the proposed exercise of discretion to limit the additional 2026/27 special levy on the personal financial advice sub-sector to $10 million, on top of its $20 million annual levy,” the submission stated.
“This is an important recognition of the cumulative financial pressure being placed on advice firms. It is, however, short-term levy relief rather than a solution to the underlying drivers of the scheme’s costs.
“The four consultation questions are necessarily concerned with how a $170.262 million shortfall is allocated. That should not allow the policy debate to become confined to who pays after the harm has occurred. The continuing increase in CSLR costs demonstrates why prevention must remain the central sustainability objective.”
The association added the waterfall framework needed greater transparency around how sub-sectors were connected, the evidence used to draw those connections and the process by which consumer losses were mapped to sub-sectors to which a levy was applied.
“The consultation paper identifies the responsible entities of managed investment schemes as the Tier 2 connected sub-sector for 2026/27, but the published material does not provide enough detail for stakeholders to reproduce the assessment, test all relevant inclusions and exclusions, or assess the distributional and viability impacts of the proposed levies,” the submission noted.
“Treasury is asking stakeholders to provide evidence about concentrated entity-level impacts and sub-sector viability while publishing only aggregate sub-sector allocations.
“Treasury and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) hold regulatory and industry-funding data that is not available to most stakeholders. A transparent special levy framework should therefore include a distributional and viability analysis prepared by the government.”
The use of CSLR levy sub-sectors was also viewed as a limited way to assess how consumer harm took place and then create levies.
“ASIC’s public material on Shield and First Guardian identifies a broader chain involving lead generators, advisers and licensees, superannuation trustees, responsible entities and other participants,” the association said.
“Some important participants, including lead generators and social media platforms used as promotion channels, do not fall within the CSLR levy. This strengthens the case for prevention reforms operating alongside, and not merely after, the funding framework.”
